quiz.title: Unit 3 SAQ 03
quiz.headline: Religious policy in the Mughal Empire
quiz.prompt: Answer all parts of the question.
quiz.instructions: Answer all three parts. For each part, Answer the question directly, Prove it with specific historical evidence, and Explain how the evidence supports your answer. On the AP exam each part earns one point. This is self-assessment practice, not official College Board scoring.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice in AP short-answer format. Model answers show one strong response; other accurate, well-supported answers can earn the point.

scaffold.label: Answer
scaffold.text: Respond directly to the task verb: identify, describe, or explain.

scaffold.label: Prove
scaffold.text: Name a specific person, place, institution, or development.

scaffold.label: Explain
scaffold.text: Show how or why the evidence answers the question.

parts.prompt: Identify ONE policy by which the Mughal emperor Akbar tried to win the support of his non-Muslim subjects.
criteria: Connects it to non-Muslim, especially Hindu, subjects.

model.answer: Akbar ended the jizya, the tax paid by non-Muslims.
model.prove: He abolished the jizya in 1564, and he also appointed Hindu Rajput leaders to high ranks in the imperial service.
model.explain: Removing the tax and opening high offices gave Hindu elites a stake in Mughal rule and helped Akbar govern a population that was mostly Hindu.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also identify his policy of sulh-i-kul, or “peace with all,” his marriages to Rajput princesses, or his sponsorship of discussions among scholars of different faiths.

parts.prompt: Describe ONE way the religious policies of Akbar's great-grandson Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) differed from Akbar's.
criteria: Names a specific policy of Aurangzeb.
Describes how it differed from Akbar's approach.

model.answer: Aurangzeb reimposed the jizya on non-Muslims.
model.prove: In 1679 he restored the tax that Akbar had abolished, and he ordered some Hindu temples destroyed.
model.explain: These measures emphasized the privileged position of Islam and ended Akbar's effort to treat Hindus as full partners in the state.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also describe Aurangzeb's execution of the Sikh guru Tegh Bahadur in 1675 or his stricter enforcement of Islamic law.

parts.prompt: Explain ONE way religious policy affected the stability of the Mughal Empire in the late 1600s and early 1700s.
criteria: Names a specific group, region, or event.
Explains how religious policy contributed to instability.

model.answer: Stricter policies contributed to revolts that weakened the empire.
model.prove: The Marathas under Shivaji and his successors resisted Mughal rule in the Deccan, and Sikhs under Guru Gobind Singh organized as a military community after the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur.
model.explain: Aurangzeb's long wars against these groups drained the treasury and army, and after his death in 1707 the Mughal state lost control of many provinces.

parts.alternatives: Answers can also explain Rajput resentment of Aurangzeb's policies or the empire's loss of Hindu allies who had been central to Akbar's system.
